The idea, the reason, and the ambition

About the Project
& Why It Exists

A picture is a beginning, not a boundary.

We learn more confidently when new ideas have somewhere to belong. But genuine mathematical understanding also asks us to go beyond what we can see.

The Rectangle Paradigm is built around both sides of that belief. It uses one familiar object—the rectangle—to offer students a first mental picture of many mathematical ideas, then encourages them to question that picture, express what they have discovered, and eventually reason without needing a diagram at all.

01 · The reason02 · The common languageOur learning philosophy03 · The power and its limits04 · The long-term vision05 · How to use the archiveProject credits

01 · The reason

Why a mental picture matters

When we get to know a person, we do not memorize every action or emotion independently. Over time, our observations form a general picture that helps us make sense of what happens next. Learning mathematics can work in a similar way. An early mental model gives unfamiliar definitions, symbols, and calculations somewhere to fit.

Imagine hearing a complicated account of a family disagreement involving relatives you have never met. You spend so much effort working out who said what to whom that the larger story is difficult to follow. If you already know the people and the situation, you can concentrate on the important details. A helpful mathematical picture offers that same sense of orientation.

A student who understands the question a topic is trying to answer can return to that purpose when the calculations become difficult. They may not yet follow every step, but they know what the steps are for. This project exists to offer that initial orientation—not as a shortcut around mathematics, but as a reason to keep exploring it.

02 · The common language

Why begin with the area of a rectangle?

The rectangle is one of the earliest geometric models students meet. Its area, A = base × height, gives multiplication a shape. More importantly, that shape can be divided, rearranged, scaled, compared, and refined without losing track of what its parts mean.

A grid of small rectangles can explain multiplication and equivalent fractions. Rearranged pieces can reveal algebraic identities. Repeated partitions can illuminate finite and infinite series. A probability space can be represented by proportional regions, while increasingly thin rectangles offer a way into integration. One familiar idea becomes a bridge between subjects that otherwise seem unrelated.

Not every topic in this archive is literally a rectangular dissection; some use the broader language of area, comparison, coordinate geometry, or limiting constructions. Their shared aim is to make the mathematical relationship visible before asking the learner to handle its most compressed symbolic form.

Our learning philosophy

See it. Explain it. Go beyond it.

  1. See the relationship.

    Begin with a diagram you can explore. Notice the pieces, their proportions, and what changes when you move them.

  2. Put the picture into words and symbols.

    Explain which areas are equal, why a comparison works, and what assumptions the construction needs. Connect those observations to an equation or an argument.

  3. Test the idea beyond the drawing.

    Change the values, investigate edge cases, or ask whether the argument still holds when the picture is difficult—or impossible—to draw.

03 · The power and its limits

The picture is a map, not the territory

Visual intuition is powerful precisely because it simplifies. But every picture leaves something out. A diagram may show only one special case; it may hide an assumption about positive lengths; it may suggest a pattern without establishing that the pattern always holds. And some mathematical objects are too abstract or too high-dimensional to fit an ordinary spatial image.

Think of the real number line. It is a remarkably useful way to imagine order, distance, intervals, and limits, even though the mathematical structure of the real numbers is richer than any line we can literally draw. The model helps us begin; definitions and proofs help us discover what is actually true.

This archive therefore does not claim that every picture is automatically a proof. A convincing visual argument must still account for its assumptions, explain why its construction works, and show that its conclusion holds in the intended setting. The drawing should lead to those questions, not replace them.

“I do not have a picture for this yet, but I can still work with it.”

That confidence is as important as the ability to visualize.

04 · The long-term vision

Growing beyond our first intuition

At more advanced levels, mathematics will ask students to work with ideas that resist visualization. It is natural for an unfamiliar definition or proof to feel opaque at first. Understanding can also arrive later—through examples, counterexamples, repeated use, discussion, and formal arguments that gradually become familiar.

The hope is that intuitive and formal understanding eventually reinforce each other. A picture can suggest what might be true; algebra and proof can tell us exactly when and why it is true; new abstract insights can, in turn, improve the picture we began with.

The goal is not to make students dependent on diagrams. It is to help them build enough confidence, curiosity, and structural understanding to move beyond those diagrams when the mathematics demands it.

05 · A note to learners and teachers

How to use this archive

Choose a topic you already know—or one that currently feels abstract. Open its interactive proof and try to understand the geometry before looking for a formula. Ask yourself:

  • What is being represented by each length, region, or movement?
  • What stays the same when the shape is partitioned or rearranged?
  • Can I explain the result without pointing at the screen?
  • What assumptions does this demonstration make, and when might it fail?

Then compare your explanation with the symbolic statement. Return to the visual model when it helps, and set it aside when your reasoning no longer needs it. Whether you are meeting multiplication for the first time or exploring a theorem in calculus, the habit is the same: move deliberately between what you can see and what you can justify.

References & inspiration

Bibliography
& References

A lineage of visual mathematical reasoning

This project draws inspiration from visual proofs, mathematical problem solving, and classical geometric methods. The following works and traditions have helped shape its approach. Some are indirect inspirations; the additional reading offers ways to explore the ideas further.

  1. Roger B. Nelsen

    Proofs Without Words III: Further Exercises in Visual Thinking

    A collection of mathematical arguments communicated through carefully constructed diagrams.

    Book information ↗

  2. Martin Gardner

    Writings on recreational mathematics

    Geometric dissections, patterns, and surprising connections between elementary pictures and deeper mathematical ideas. Gardner’s books and columns are part of the project’s wider inspiration.

    Explore Gardner’s books ↗

  3. Historical background

    Classical area methods

    Cavalieri-style slicing, lattice counting, and dissection arguments that anticipate integration and measure. This entry names a mathematical tradition rather than a single source.

  4. George Pólya

    How to Solve It: A New Aspect of Mathematical Method

    Heuristic reasoning and mathematical problem solving, including the importance of representation, analogy, and working backward from structure.

    Book information ↗

  5. Diophantus

    Numerical identities and equations

    Classical work on equations and numerical identities, including identities connected to sums of squares. Included as historical inspiration.

  6. David Hilbert and Stefan Cohn-Vossen

    Geometry and the Imagination

    Geometric insight and visual approaches to mathematical ideas.

  7. Richard Courant and Herbert Robbins

    What Is Mathematics?

    An exploration of mathematical concepts and the intuition and reasoning behind them.

  8. Euclid · Historical background and further reading

    Elements, Book II

    Classical relationships between rectangles and squares. David Joyce’s online edition offers a way to study the propositions and their constructions.

    Read Book II ↗

  9. Charles C. Pugh

    Real Mathematical Analysis

    A study of real analysis that connects careful proofs with pictures and geometric intuition.

    Read the book (PDF) ↗
How these references are used
